title: Job 16:18–22
context: Job continues speaking. He calls on the earth not to cover his blood and asks that his cry find no resting place, an image that recalls the blood of Abel crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Then he declares that even now his witness is in heaven and the one who vouches for him is on high, someone who would maintain the right of a man with God. Interpreters differ on who this witness is: God himself, appealed to against God as Job experiences him; a heavenly mediator distinct from God; or Job’s own cry personified. Job has already wished for an umpire (Job 9:33) and will later speak of his Redeemer (Job 19:25). The line translated my friends scoff at me in verse 20 can also be read in Hebrew as speaking of an intercessor or spokesman as Job’s friend, which bears on the witness question; translations differ. A Christological application, hearing in the witness a pointer to Christ the one mediator and advocate (compare 1 Timothy 2:5; 1 John 2:1; Hebrews 7:25), is commonly made in both Arminian and Reformed traditions, as a reading of the passage in light of the whole Bible rather than a claim the text makes on its own. The unit ends with Job expecting to go the way of no return in a few years.

verses.text: “Earth, don’t cover my blood. Let my cry have no place to rest.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job asking the earth not to cover his blood and his cry not to rest. He wants his case to remain open before heaven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of Abel’s blood crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Both traditions commonly read the verse as Job’s demand that injustice not be forgotten.

verses.text: Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven. He who vouches for me is on high.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job declaring that his witness is in heaven and the one who vouches for him is on high. They commonly hold the witness’s identity with care, whether God himself or a heavenly mediator.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a remarkable turn toward hope in the midst of complaint. Many in both traditions commonly apply the verse to Christ as advocate (compare 1 John 2:1), as a reading in light of the whole Bible rather than the text’s plain claim.

verses.text: My friends scoff at me. My eyes pour out tears to God,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying his friends scoff while his eyes pour out tears to God. He turns from human scorn to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job appealing to the very God he has just described as afflicting him. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as tears offered to God even while he seems distant.

verses.text: that he would maintain the right of a man with God, of a son of man with his neighbor!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job longing for someone to maintain the right of a man with God, as one would for a neighbor. He seeks a fair hearing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the longing for a mediator that Job voiced earlier (Job 9:33). Both traditions commonly hear in it a hope later fulfilled in Christ (compare 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 7:25), labeled as a reading.

verses.text: For when a few years have come, I will go the way of no return.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job expecting to go the way of no return after a few years. He feels time running out for his vindication.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job’s sense of mortality pressing his plea (compare Job 10:21). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of his urgent appeal, not a full statement on the afterlife.
